scenes.spec: parking lot, slow full-lock turn, window down
scenes.narration: Roll through a parking lot with the wheel cranked, window down, and your car performs its little concert: maybe a click-click-click, maybe a groan, maybe a whine that follows the wheel. Straighten out — silence. Turning is when your front end works hardest: joints articulate to their limits, weight shifts onto one side, and parts that pass the straight-line test get cross-examined. Which is great news for diagnosis — because each part fails with its own *specific sound*. This episode is an ear-training course: five noises, five names, five very different bills.

scenes.spec: channel card — "Why Is My Car Doing That?"
sound-map card — "CLICKING in tight turns" / "HUM/GROWL in sweeping turns" / "WHINE with the wheel" / "CLUNK over bumps while turning" / "CREAK/GROAN low speed"
scenes.narration: Five sounds, and WHEN each speaks: (parking lots, U-turns) when you swing the wheel the other way especially at full lock Match your noise now; the causes below run in that order.

scenes.section: CAUSE #1 — CLICKING: THE CV JOINT (the parking-lot drumbeat)
scenes.spec: NEW 3D — CV axle: shaft, constant-velocity joint ball cage, rubber boot; boot torn, grease flung, grit inside
scenes.narration: Front-wheel-drive cars send power through **CV (constant velocity) joints** — caged ball bearings that let the axle bend with steering and suspension while spinning. Each lives inside a rubber **boot** full of grease. The boot tears with age, grease flings out, grit gets in, and the dry joint starts announcing tight turns: *click-click-click* in time with wheel speed. The inspection beat: a torn boot with flung grease is visible with a flashlight behind the front wheels — and caught at TORN-BOOT stage (before the clicking starts) it's a cheap reboot job instead of an axle. Clicking already? The joint's eating itself; axle replacement territory, and the noise only grows. [TECH CONFIRM — do you still reboot caught-early joints, or is replacement-axle-always the modern economics? Your boot-inspection interval advice]

scenes.section: CAUSE #2 — HUM/GROWL IN SWEEPING TURNS: THE WHEEL BEARING RETURNS
scenes.spec: hub/bearing from ep 1 — load shifting onto outer wheel in a sweeper; growl waves loudest with weight on the bad side
scenes.narration: Episode 3's impostor gets its turn as the headliner. In a sweeping turn, the car's weight rolls onto the outside wheel — and a worn bearing under load hums, growls, or roars. The steering-input version of the S-weave test: noise that gets LOUDER turning one direction and QUIETER the other names the loaded side. [TECH CONFIRM — restate: the noisy-when-loaded side is the bad bearing, correct? People get this backwards constantly] Bearing urgency recap from ep 3 applies: loud bearings are a today-not-someday item — wheels depend on them. [TECH CONFIRM — has FHT seen a genuinely failed/separated bearing case worth a 10-second cautionary mention?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #3 — WHINE WITH THE WHEEL: POWER STEERING
scenes.spec: steering path — pump (hydraulic) pulling fluid, whining at low level/full lock; EPS note for electric cars
scenes.narration: A whine that tracks your steering input — worse the further you turn, loudest at full lock — is the **power steering pump** talking (hydraulic systems): low fluid, aerated fluid, or a tired pump. Check the reservoir; a foamy, low, or burnt fluid tells the story, and full-lock-held-too-long is genuinely hard on pumps. Electric-assist cars (most new ones) skip the pump — their version is usually a column/rack noise or motor complaint, different sound family. [TECH CONFIRM — the hydraulic-vs-EPS split in FHT's actual fleet mix; worth tailoring emphasis?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #4 — CLUNK OVER BUMPS WHILE TURNING: LINKS, TIE RODS, BALL JOINTS
scenes.spec: suspension corner — sway bar end link loose, tie rod end play, ball joint worn; clunk on articulation
scenes.narration: The clunk family lives where suspension meets steering: **sway bar end links** (the most common cheap clunk), **tie rod ends**, and **ball joints**. Turning plus a bump articulates everything at once, and worn joints knock in their sockets. Ep 1's suspension section is cousins with this one — vague steering and wandering often ride along. The shop test is play-checking with the wheel jacked up; the serious end (separating ball joint or tie rod) is a lose-steering-control failure mode, which is why clunks earn prompt inspections even though most turn out to be the cheap link. [TECH CONFIRM — link vs tie rod vs ball joint frequency; bless the urgency framing]

scenes.section: CAUSE #5 — CREAK AND GROAN: BUSHINGS, MOUNTS, AND THE SPRING SEAT
scenes.spec: strut top mount rotating with a dry groan; control arm bushings cracked; spring seat creak
scenes.narration: The ship-noise tier: **strut top mounts** (the bearing your whole strut pivots on when steering) groan and creak when dry or worn — classic low-speed, full-lock, worse-cold pattern. Aged **control-arm bushings** creak over the same moves. Annoying more than dangerous, usually — but a seized strut mount also ruins steering return and tire wear, so it's a fix-with-the-next-job item, not a never item. scenes.section: THE REPAIR — WHAT THE MONEY LOOKS LIKE
scenes.narration: Rough ladder, cheapest first: sway bar links and boot re-greases at the bottom; tie rods, strut mounts, power-steering service in the middle; CV axles and bearings mid-to-upper; ball joints varying by design. The alignment footnote: anything that touches steering geometry — tie rods especially — ends with an **alignment**, so that line on the quote isn't padding. scenes.spec: three-tier verdict card — "Schedule it" / "This week" / "Inspect before highway"
scenes.narration: **Schedule it:** creaks and groans, mild PS whine with a healthy reservoir top-up. Comfort-tier, on your calendar. **This week:** clicking CV joints (they only get worse and can strand you), recurring clunks, foamy/burnt PS fluid. **Inspect before highway driving:** loud/growing bearing noise, any clunk with visible steering play or wandering, or a click that's become a shudder under power. Steering and wheel-retention parts get the conservative call, every time. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the tiers]

So: the turn is the interrogation, and the sound is the confession. Clicks name the CV joint, sweeping growls name the loaded bearing, wheel-tracking whines name the pump, bump-clunks name the linkage, and ship-creaks name the mounts. Five sounds, five parts, and a flashlight check of the boots that can catch the expensive one while it's cheap. Next time: the scariest pedal sensation there is — your brake pedal goes further than it should — and the hydraulic story behind it.
